cap: The gland hangs from the skin by Cooper ligaments and rests on the pectoral fascia, separated from it by the loose retromammary space. Ducts from each lobule widen into a lactiferous sinus and open on the nipple. That layering explains two exam signs: tumor that shortens Cooper ligaments dimples the skin, and tumor that crosses the retromammary space fixes the mass to the chest wall.
teach: Read the figure from the bottom up. Ribs and pectoralis major form the chest wall; the pectoral fascia covers the muscle; the retromammary space is the gliding plane; the gland and its fat sit in the subcutaneous tissue under the skin. Each labeled layer is a plane a carcinoma can reach, and each gives a different exam sign.
